sections.title: What is a Segment Tree?
sections.content:
A Segment Tree is a binary tree built over an array, where each node stores an aggregated result (sum, min, max, GCD, etc.) for a contiguous range of the array. A leaf node represents a single element. An internal node represents the union of its children's ranges. The root covers the full array [0, n-1].

This structure answers **range queries** - "what is the sum/min/max of elements from index l to r?" - in O(log n), and handles **point updates** - "change arr[i] to a new value" - also in O(log n). The key strength is supporting *both* simultaneously.

Compare to prefix sums: prefix sums answer range sum in O(1) but cannot handle updates efficiently (an update requires O(n) to recompute the prefix array). Segment trees sacrifice the O(1) query constant for O(log n) updates, making them the default when your problem involves both queries and mutations.

With **lazy propagation**, segment trees extend to handle **range updates** (e.g., add 5 to all elements in [l, r]) while keeping both updates and queries at O(log n). This makes them one of the most versatile data structures in competitive programming and technical interviews.

sections.title: When to Use This
sections.content: Use a segment tree when your problem requires repeatedly querying an aggregate (sum, min, max, GCD, count) over a range of an array *and* the array can be updated between queries. If the array is static (no updates), prefix sums are simpler and faster. If updates are only point updates, a basic segment tree without lazy works. If updates are range updates (add/set a value across a range), you need lazy propagation.
signals: range minimum or maximum with updates
count elements in range satisfying a condition

sections.title: Core Concepts
sections.content:
## Tree Structure and Indexing

For an array of size `n`, a segment tree needs up to `4n` nodes stored in a **1-indexed array**. Node `1` is the root, covering `[0, n-1]`. For a node at index `p` covering range `[l, r]`, compute `mid = Math.floor((l + r) / 2)`. Its left child is at index `2p` covering `[l, mid]`, and its right child is at `2p + 1` covering `[mid+1, r]`. Leaf nodes satisfy `l === r`. Always allocate `4 * n` space to safely handle non-power-of-2 sizes.

## Build, Query, Update

**Build** - recursively build left and right subtrees, then combine: `tree[p] = tree[2p] + tree[2p+1]` (for sum). The identity element depends on the operation: `0` for sum, `Infinity` for min, `-Infinity` for max. Build runs in O(n).

**Query(l, r)** - check three cases at each node: (1) current range is fully inside `[l, r]` → return node value; (2) fully outside `[l, r]` → return identity; (3) partial overlap → recurse into both children and combine results. O(log n).

**Update(i, val)** - walk down to leaf `i`, update it, then update all ancestors on the path back up by recomputing from children. O(log n).

## Lazy Propagation

Needed when you have **range updates** (e.g., add 5 to all elements in `[l, r]`). Without lazy, applying a range update naively touches all leaves in the range: O(n). Lazy stores a "pending" update at each node that is **pushed down to children only when needed**. When you query or update and need to go deeper, first flush the lazy value to both children. This defers work and keeps range updates at O(log n).

## Generalization to Other Operations

The operation stored in each node can be anything **associative**: GCD, product (mod some prime), maximum frequency in a subarray, XOR, etc. The combine step just changes. The structure and traversal remain identical.

sections.title: Core Template
sections.explanation: Builds a sum segment tree over an array and supports O(log n) point updates and O(log n) range sum queries. Replace the combine step (`+`) and identity (`0`) to adapt to min, max, GCD, or any associative operation.

items.name: Lazy Propagation
items.description: Extends the basic segment tree to handle range updates (add/set a value across [l, r]) in O(log n). Each node carries a `lazy` value representing a pending update not yet pushed to children. Before descending, push the lazy value down.
items.example_problem: Range Sum Query - Mutable (with range updates)

items.name: Persistent Segment Tree
items.description: Each update creates a new version of the tree by copying only the O(log n) nodes on the update path, leaving the rest shared. Allows querying historical versions of the array. Used for range kth-smallest and offline queries.
items.example_problem: Count of Smaller Numbers After Self

items.name: Merge Sort Tree
items.description: Each node stores a sorted array of all elements in its range instead of a single aggregate. Enables order-statistic queries like 'how many elements in [l, r] are less than x' in O(log² n). Space is O(n log n).

items.name: 2D Segment Tree
items.description: A segment tree of segment trees for 2D range queries (e.g., sum/min/max in a sub-rectangle of a matrix with point updates). Query and update are O(log² n). Space and build time are O(n² log n) in the naive form.

sections.title: Complexity
sections.time: O(n) build, O(log n) query, O(log n) update
sections.explanation: Build visits every node once: 2n - 1 nodes total, so O(n). Each query/update traverses at most one path from root to leaf (height = log n), plus at each level potentially splits into two paths for query - but the total nodes visited per query is still O(log n) because at each level we enter at most 2 nodes total (the O(4 log n) bound). Space is O(4n) = O(n) for the flat node array.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
items: Allocating only `2n` nodes instead of `4n` - for non-power-of-2 array sizes, the recursive indexing can reach indices up to `4n`, causing silent out-of-bounds writes and wrong answers.

Using the wrong identity element in queries - for sum use `0`, for min use `Infinity`, for max use `-Infinity`. Using `0` as identity for a min-query means empty ranges return `0` instead of infinity, corrupting the answer when combining with real values.
Lazy propagation: not pushing lazy to children before recursing into them - querying children without flushing their pending updates returns stale node values.
0-indexed vs 1-indexed confusion - segment tree nodes are 1-indexed (root at index 1), but array elements are 0-indexed. Passing array indices directly as node indices causes wrong tree navigation.

Off-by-one in mid calculation - always use `Math.floor((l + r) / 2)`, left child covers `[l, mid]`, right covers `[mid+1, r]`. Using `mid = (l+r+1)/2` for left child causes infinite recursion on some ranges.

sections.title: What to Learn Next
sections.why: Fenwick Trees solve a subset of segment tree problems (prefix sum with point updates) with simpler code and better constant factors. Understanding both lets you pick the lighter tool when it fits, and reinforces the bit manipulation behind BIT indexing.
